title: Introduction to Bridges and Articulation Points
description: Find the single edges and nodes whose removal disconnects a graph

sections.title: 12. Pitfalls and How to Approach It

blocks.text: In an undirected graph, some connections are more critical than others. A bridge is an edge whose removal breaks the graph into pieces, and an articulation point is a node whose removal does the same.
These are the weak points of a network. Finding them tells you where a single failure would cut connectivity, and a clever depth first search finds them all in one linear pass.

blocks.caption: A bridge edge and an articulation point are the graph single points of failure
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761803-621169322.png

By the end of this topic you will understand both definitions, why they matter, the naive approach and why it is slow, and the elegant discovery time and low link method that finds every bridge and articulation point efficiently. It is a classic application of DFS.
Both concepts share one engine: a DFS that records when each node was first seen and how far back its subtree can climb. Master that engine and both fall out at once.
They are defined for undirected graphs, where the question of an alternate route makes clean sense.

An articulation point, also called a cut vertex, is a node whose removal increases the number of disconnected pieces in the graph. Take it out, along with its edges, and part of the graph becomes unreachable from the rest.

blocks.caption: Removing an articulation point splits the graph into separate pieces
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761804-536091523.png
Intuitively, an articulation point is a chokepoint: all traffic between two parts of the graph must pass through it. Remove it, and those parts are severed.

items: A single node whose removal disconnects the graph
Also known as a cut vertex
It is a chokepoint that traffic must pass through
A graph may have zero, one, or many of them

blocks.text: In the example graph, node D is an articulation point: everything to its right depends on passing through it, so removing D strands that side.

items: A cut vertex, another name for the same thing
Its removal raises the count of components
All paths between two regions funnel through it
A cycle around a node protects it from being critical

blocks.text: A bridge, also called a cut edge, is the edge version of the same idea. It is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph, or increases the number of components.

blocks.caption: Removing a bridge edge splits the graph into two pieces
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761804-491295626.png
A bridge is the only link between two otherwise separate regions. There is no alternate route around it, so cutting it isolates one side from the other.

The defining test:

An edge is a bridge exactly when it lies on no cycle. If some cycle contains the edge, there is an alternate path, so removing it cannot disconnect anything.
In the same example, the edge from C to D is a bridge: it is the sole connection between the left triangle and the right side.
Edges inside the triangle are not bridges, because the cycle gives an alternate route around each of them.
So the quick mental test is cycles: an edge on some cycle is never a bridge, and an edge on no cycle always is.
Bridges and articulation points identify the fragile parts of any network, which is enormously useful for reliability and design.

items: In a computer network, they are the links and routers whose failure splits the network
In a road map, they are the roads and junctions whose closure isolates a town
In infrastructure, they reveal where to add redundancy
In graph analysis, they mark the boundaries between tightly knit clusters

blocks.text: Knowing them lets engineers reinforce exactly the spots that matter, rather than guessing where the network is vulnerable.
The common theme is a single point of failure. Bridges and articulation points are precisely the elements a resilient design wants to eliminate or duplicate.

Resilience in one idea:

A network with no bridges and no articulation points survives any single failure. Finding them tells you exactly where redundancy is missing.
The obvious way to find these weak points is to test each one directly. For every edge, remove it and check whether the graph is still connected; for every node, do the same.
This works, but it is slow. Each connectivity check is a full traversal, and you repeat it once per edge or node, giving a cost proportional to the number of elements times the size of the graph.

items: Remove each edge or node one at a time
Run a traversal to test if the graph is still connected
If it is not, that element is a bridge or articulation point
Correct, but far too slow for large graphs

blocks.text: We want to find everything in a single traversal instead, and that is exactly what the low link method achieves.
Concretely, removing each of E edges and running an O(V plus E) check gives roughly O(E times (V plus E)), which is far too slow for large graphs.
The low link method replaces all of that repeated work with a single clever traversal.
The efficient approach runs one depth first search and, as it explores, works out whether each edge or node is critical using two timestamps per node.

blocks.caption: Discovery time and low link together reveal every bridge and articulation point
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761805-97734324.png

The key question is whether a subtree explored by the DFS has any back edge that climbs to an ancestor. If it does, there is an alternate route, so the connection is not critical. If it does not, the connection is a bridge or articulation point.

Back edges are escape routes:

A back edge from a subtree up to an ancestor is an alternate path. Its presence or absence is what decides whether an edge or node is critical.
As the DFS descends, it builds a tree of the graph, and the non tree connections it meets are back edges to ancestors.
Those back edges are the alternate routes, and tracking the highest one each subtree can reach is the whole trick.
This is the same low link technique that powers Tarjan strongly connected components, reused here for the undirected case.
Give every node two numbers during the DFS. The discovery time is the step at which the node was first visited, so it increases as the search goes deeper.
The low link of a node is the smallest discovery time reachable from that node subtree, including through a single back edge. It answers how far back up the tree this subtree can escape.

items: disc[u]: the timestamp when u was first visited
low[u]: the earliest node reachable from u subtree, via tree and one back edge
A child with a small low link can escape above its parent
A child that cannot escape signals a critical connection

blocks.text: Computing the low link is easy: start it equal to the discovery time, then lower it using back edges and the low links of children as the DFS returns.
You update low[u] in two places: from a back edge directly to an ancestor, and from the low link of each child as the recursion returns.
The final low link therefore summarises the best escape available to the entire subtree rooted at u.
For a tree edge from u to its child v, the edge is a bridge exactly when the low link of v is strictly greater than the discovery time of u.

blocks.caption: A tree edge is a bridge when the child subtree cannot reach at or above the parent
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761805-992145848.png
This condition means v and everything below it has no back edge reaching u or any earlier node. So the only way to reach that subtree is through this one edge, which makes it a bridge.
Trace the condition: if low[v] is greater than disc[u], nothing under v can reach u or above, so cutting the u to v edge isolates that subtree.
If instead a back edge let low[v] reach disc[u] or lower, an alternate route exists and the edge is safe.

Articulation points use almost the same machinery, with a slightly softer condition. For a non root node u with a child v, u is an articulation point when the low link of v is greater than or equal to the discovery time of u.
The difference from a bridge is the equality. If v can climb back to u itself but no higher, the edge is not a bridge, yet u is still a chokepoint, because removing u would cut v subtree off.

items: For a non root u with child v, u is an articulation point if low[v] is at least disc[u]
The greater than or equal test differs from the strict test for bridges
A back edge reaching u but not above it still makes u critical
The root of the DFS needs a special rule

blocks.text: The intuition is that a chokepoint node holds up a subtree that cannot escape past it, even if that subtree can loop back to the node itself.

items: Non root u is critical if some child v has low[v] at least disc[u]
That means v subtree cannot bypass u
The bridge test is the strict version of this test
The root is handled by counting its children

blocks.text: The starting node of the DFS, the root, needs its own rule, because it has no parent and no discovery time above it to compare against.
The root is an articulation point if and only if it has more than one child in the DFS tree. With two or more separate subtrees, removing the root disconnects them from each other.

Do not forget the root:

The most common bug in articulation point code is mishandling the root. Count its DFS children and mark it critical only when it has at least two.
The reason is simple: the root has no ancestor to be cut off from, so it only matters whether it holds together multiple independent subtrees.
With a single child, removing the root leaves that one subtree intact and still connected internally.

The number one bug:

Forgetting the root rule. Always count the DFS children of the start node and flag it only when it has two or more.
The whole method is a single depth first search with constant extra work per edge, which makes it optimal.

items: Time: O(V plus E), one DFS over the graph
Space: O(V) for the discovery and low link arrays plus the recursion stack
Far better than the naive O(V times (V plus E)) remove and test approach
Both bridges and articulation points can be found in the same pass

blocks.text: Linear time means you can analyse even very large networks for their weak points quickly.
Because it is a single DFS, the analysis is the same as any traversal: touch every node once and every edge a constant number of times.
This makes weak point detection cheap enough to run routinely on large infrastructure graphs.
These weak point detectors are used wherever connectivity and reliability matter.

items: Finding single points of failure in computer and communication networks
Identifying critical roads or junctions in transport maps
Deciding where to add redundant links for fault tolerance
Decomposing a graph into biconnected components

blocks.text: The last use, biconnected components, groups the graph into pieces that have no internal articulation point, which builds directly on this analysis.

items: Single points of failure in networks
Critical roads and junctions in transport
Where to add redundant links
Biconnected component decomposition

content.title: 12. Pitfalls and How to Approach It

blocks.text: A few details are essential to get right.

items: Handle the DFS root separately, marking it critical only with two or more children
Skip the edge back to the immediate parent, but be careful with duplicate edges
Use a strict greater than for bridges and a greater than or equal for articulation points
Run the DFS from every unvisited node so disconnected graphs are fully covered

blocks.text:
How to spot these problems:

Look for questions about which single link or node would break connectivity, or about critical connections. That phrasing points straight at bridges and articulation points.
Watch out for multi edges between the same pair of nodes: two parallel edges mean neither is a bridge, so skipping only the immediate parent is not always enough.
Bridges and articulation points pinpoint exactly where a graph is fragile.

items: A bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph
An articulation point is a node whose removal disconnects the graph
A single DFS with discovery times and low links finds them all
A tree edge is a bridge when low[v] is greater than disc[u]
The DFS root is an articulation point only with two or more children

blocks.text: Whenever you need to know which single failure would break a network, run the low link DFS and it reveals every critical edge and node in one pass.
Remember the picture: a lone edge or node with no cycle around it, holding two regions together, is exactly the thing whose removal splits the graph.
